speaker: The Chairman
text: Head S, Ministry of Manpower, Mr Desmond Choo.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head S of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Since the start of the pandemic, the MOM has been charged with protecting the workforce from escalating unemployment and the threat of COVID as workers returned to work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To further judge the Ministry’s progress, it is perhaps instructive to examine much of our post-recovery Budget debate thus far.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We had the chance to look at many longer term plans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But this would not likely have happened if our unemployment rates have tanked and not recovered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This stands in stark contrast to many overseas countries which are still deeply mired in COVID-19 cases and in the deepest of recession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So many thanks to Minister Josephine Teo and her team of MOM officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even so, we know that we are not out of the woods and recovery is far from certain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are always a big cluster or two away from falling off the recessionary cliff.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, the aviation, aerospace, hospitality and retail sectors still have years before they can recover.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Much time, and rightly so, were spent debating supporting our lower wage workers in the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key trend in many other countries has been the disproportionate number of lower income workers losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If these jobs are lost, then uplifting lower wage workers will only be doubly difficult.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: That we are able to moderate unemployment rates and maintain industrial peace even during very difficult times is not a matter of good fortune.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The secret weapon we have is our special model of tripartism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers and companies are united with the Government to implement difficult cost-cutting measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has allowed us to manage costs and save jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I remembered representing the unions in the many prolonged and tense National Wage Council discussions last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While understandably tense and sometimes heated, we were united in trust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: That we would do our best to ensure the Singapore economy will survive and as many workers as possible remain in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that while we look at refining manpower policies, we do not forget tripartism, Singapore's bulwark against debilitating economic forces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has worked during every one of our crises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has worked during the deepest of the COVID pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to continue to safeguard and invest in it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has surfaced the highly disruptive forces of digitalisation and remote working.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It goes just beyond workers in Singapore being dislocated but also losing jobs permanently because of the ease of working online.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our decades-long investment in our training and placement system has allowed us to re-deploy workers quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the Labour Movement, we know the difficulty of retraining and finding worker another job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to a New York Times article on 27 February 2021, unemployment is traumatic, affecting mental and physical health, and also erodes skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We see that with our very own retrenched workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A robust placement system is critical not only during this crisis but also to tackle structural dislocations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry continue to evolve our job placement system to deal with structural changes, especially for our PMEs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The structural forces also beg the question on how shall we evolve our foreign manpower system so that it serves both current and future needs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has served companies well over the years as they could expand beyond our small local workforce size would allow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question going ahead is how to help businesses to operate effectively while at the same time, allowing for the Singaporean Core to grow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can be difficult to tighten manpower quota without causing disruption to many companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Industries are more complex now and so are their needs for manpower and talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many companies are involved in multiple industries and do not neatly fall into the five major sectors in the current system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies also need multi-skilled workers doing multiple roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we have critical shortages of local workers in some industries, our local workforce might have supply in many other places.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And this can happen within the same sector amongst different job roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is not surprising considering how our educational and workforce profiles have changed rapidly over recent years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry balance such needs going forward?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has also brought to the spotlight an important part of our workforce – which is the Self-Employed Persons (SEPs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SIRS was instrumental in helping our SEPs tide through a very difficult period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I had shared during the Budget debate on the need to level the playing field between the SEPs and the big platform companies and organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a tricky trade-off to manage between their take-home income and preparing for the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry also involve the companies to provide for these SEPs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, many SEPs are not given training and are likely to be stagnant and lose productivity over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we continue to develop and provide training for SEPs so that we can grow this segment of the workforce?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to touch on our foreign domestic workers (FDWs) and how we can care for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has a network of 1,000 volunteers and ambassadors who engage with them to identify those who require assistance, educate them about their rights, and about resources.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This figure is worrying as these are supposed to be workers in executive and managerial positions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There is, therefore, a need to examine closer to see if these are actually disguised PMEs, that is, given inflated titles but the job is not, effectively, a PME job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, we may have to embark on the Progressive Wage Model for such PMEs to help them in their skill, wage and career progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Similarly, we may need to, again, review the salary limit of $2,600 in Part IV of the Employment Act, and for MOM to closely monitor non time-based underemployment in Singapore despite its subjectivity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second cut, review of the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Industrial Relations Act was amended in 2015 to permit rank-and-file unions to collectively represent executive employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To avoid conflicts of interest and undermining management effectiveness, executives with senior management functions were excluded from collective representation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These functions are set out in section 17(3) of the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the years that have followed, unions which have sought to extend their scope of representation to include executives have met with some difficulties because the exclusions set out in section 17(3) are too broadly worded, thereby giving employers the opportunity to claim that even low- and mid-level executive employees fall within them, whereas the intent behind the law was only to exclude those who are at senior management levels and carrying out functions which genuinely give rise to a conflict of interest if they are represented by a union.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Besides this, there are several other procedural and technical areas which are ambiguous or need greater clarity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, it is noteworthy that this sharp reduction in employment is mostly borne by foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is more than the drop in total employment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, resident employment, mostly locals, actually grew; albeit just a modest increase of 9,300, as the various Government support measures helped push local hiring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In a way, having a foreign workforce served as a buffer and helped cushion our resident workers during an economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In better times, the foreign workforce helps businesses grow so that companies can find the workers to do the jobs that Singaporeans would not want to do.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But in a downturn, non-resident employment tends to bear the brunt as companies release their foreign workers and/or the foreign manpower restrictions start to tighten.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has been a similar experience in previous economic downturns, such as during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, it has kept our unemployment rate low, even during recessionary years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The various schemes under the Jobs Growth Incentive, or JGI, have helped to stave off massive local unemployment and also created new job openings and placements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A novel scheme that I particularly like is the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, which was intended to tackle the anticipated fallout from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Budget 2021, Deputy Prime Minister Heng listed three key enablers for our economy to emerge stronger, one of which is to develop our people and enabling Singaporeans to have good jobs and job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: He also referred to SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package as a key pillar to enable Singaporeans to learn and thrive and to seize opportunities in the new growth areas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With the package now expanded to support emerging stronger initiatives, can the Minister share the details as to how JGI can support the hiring of 200,000 locals this year and the 35,000 traineeships and training opportunities as mentioned in the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How would these hiring and training opportunities support as well as ride on the Emerging Stronger Together effort?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under the earlier phase of the JGI, 100,000 local jobseekers and 76,000 traineeships were placed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can JGI and MOM agencies help these Singaporeans transit and access new opportunities, as envisaged in the Emerging Stronger Together plans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a world where changing technology, continued globalisation and environmental considerations mean that job displacement and structural unemployment are liable to become more pervasive, co-funded PCPs of this nature will take on an increasing importance in helping our economy evolve into the competitive landscape of the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, while we have some anecdotal evidence of the programmes' benefits – a resident employer I know shares, for example, of a number of successful placements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have less systematic evidence that there is proactive re-employment of recentlydisplaced workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sort of certainty for both employer and employee is critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From the employer's perspective, it is effectively co-insurance for a risky hire since the potential employee's ability to adapt and perform in a new role is largely unknown.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From the employee's perspective, it is insurance of a different kind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The promise of a job, even if it is only guaranteed for a year, is a solid incentive to be willing to undergo uncertain and often painful re-training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would even go as far as to venture that the PCP be had not just with co-funding but to suggest that the programme become a natural extension of a more holistic unemployment insurance programme, which commences from the point of redundancy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party had previously suggested the contours of such a redundancy insurance system, which I will not repeat here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, I am making the case to further incorporate unemployment insurance, given how it is a natural complement to the PCP and JGI programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such an extended programme is not unprecedented elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sweden's Job Security Councils, for instance, receive not just standard unemployment benefits, but also financial compensation to assist in the job transition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The system seeks to provide security for a job, just not necessarily the job that you are originally trained for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Denmark's Flexisecurity encourages low-cost, flexible hiring and firing, but displaced workers receive unemployment support alongside re-training and re-education programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And Germany recently re-fashioned its National Unemployment Agency to become more of a job matching entity that issues not only career advice but also vouchers to finance re-training costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The underlying principle behind these efforts is clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is a natural end-to-end complementarity between unemployment insurance on one hand, and retraining and reintegration into the workforce on another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore already has most of the elements of an end-to-end job safety net in place, including the functional equivalent of unemployment insurance, which was widely deployed over the course of the COVID-19 crisis via a number of relief schemes and support grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All that is lacking is a willingness to institutionalise this approach and ensure that the system is cohesive so that Singaporeans unfortunate enough to be displaced from the jobs that they are previously prepared for, also receive the support and guidance they need in a tough labour market.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, if you would like to take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I will take my two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There was also a spike in part-time employment during the COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to be expected, given the economic situation, and it is encouraging that graduates are able to find some form of employment to stay productive and earn an income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, long-term underemployment would make it challenging for them to move on to better prospects, even when the economy improves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so if the part-time work they have taken on does not develop skills that are transferrable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Graduates from the lower income families and those who take loans to finance their studies are harder hit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may have to settle for any source of income that comes their way.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes informal jobs, like ride-hailing and food delivery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is unlike some of their peers who may have the privilege to be more particular with choosing their first job and spending their free time taking up courses to hone their skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is the Ministry reaching out to graduates who are working part-time jobs, especially in the informal sectors, to see how to provide targeted help to them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I notice that the focus of media reports seems to be on helping graduates from the local public Universities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about graduates from the Polytechnics, ITEs and private Universities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is their employment situation and how are they benefiting from the traineeships?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They have knowledge, skills and experience accumulated from decades of practical experience in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thanks to the Government's push for education and literacy in the earlier years, many mature workers are well-educated and possess the necessary prerequisites and qualifications to take up or transit to jobs that their younger peers qualify for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But with the labour market still tight, the challenge of landing a full-time job has been heightened.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is particularly so for the older workers, who are disadvantaged by unfair stereotypes that employers have of them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are various grants to support employers to re-design their workplace practices, processes and jobs for senior workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tripartite partners have also worked with Institutes of Higher Learning to develop a training programme specific to the management of older workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And Workforce Singapore, or WSG, introduced customised support for sectors with a higher concentration of older workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share about the progress of these efforts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the take-up among employers and how effective have they been in dispelling the myths about senior workers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some seniors prefer to work fewer hours because of health reasons, or to pursue other personal interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They built up their retirement funds and they do not need a full pay-check.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And there are also other individuals who could benefit from reduced work hours, such as care-givers and those who desire more time for other obligations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this way, we can retain more talent, including mature workers, in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share more about plans to leverage on senior employment and the mature workforce for the benefit of our economy?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, as an ageing society, the Government has cast an aspiring vision for Singaporeans to age with purpose and grace.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that providing dignified employment for elderly who are able and need to continue working will be a growing challenge in our ageing society with high cost of living.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned that a segment of our elderly may be left behind because of our fast transforming economy, especially with the rapid digitalisation of work processes by employers to increase productivity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a 70-year-old resident who came to seek employment assistance.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The resident was an experienced former security officer who was asked to retire even though she desired to continue working.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As her children were not doing well financially, she did not want to be a burden to them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She wanted an administrative or customer service role which she felt she would be adequately able to carry out.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, she said that no employers would consider her, given her age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Throughout my conversation with her, I could feel her dejected emotions because of the multiple rejections that she has been receiving.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is how elderly like the resident I mentioned, will be able to navigate skills training, job matching and job support amidst these schemes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The interest helps our CPF members to grow closer to their time and goals, which is to meet or exceed the minimum retirement sum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Now, even though 2.5% or 4% compounded over a long period of time can lead to significant interest income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, the 20- to 30-year-olds today with 30 or 40 more active working years to devote a portion of their CPF to earn higher returns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, MINDEF already has a Saver Premium Fund where investors have an option to choose between dynamic balance and stable according to the investment needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Up to 50% of the net returns from the reserve do flow back through the NIRC framework.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Could there be a more direct means by which members will be able to earn high investment returns through co-investing in the Government's investment vehicles, especially given the long time horizon for CPF monies held for our members' retirement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is already a CPF Investment Scheme in place with a list of specified investment products included under the CPFIS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should we look further when you really have the highest quality fund managers in the Government's investment vehicles and does it not make sense to allow Singaporeans to directly benefit from the Government's prudent and astute investment capabilities?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, this pandemic has seen many workers either had to take pay cuts or even lose their jobs, including the executives and management.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For the fortunate ones, they were able to move from one job to a similar, if not better job, in a shorter time compared to others.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This was made easier with the collective efforts of various agencies including NTUC's Job Security Council to help secure jobs for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For some, who are unable to find employment opportunities, they had to take on alternative temporary jobs to tide them over such as driving private hire vehicles or working as food delivery persons.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What were the bottlenecks that stop an individual and/or employers from recruiting the displaced workers through programmes such as PCP?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: How many of those who went through such programs have resulted in taking on higher value added jobs or new job areas?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, how can such programmes be effectively marketed for better outreach so that we can entice self-employed workers such as private hire drivers or those working in a gig economy to join the permanent workforce for better job security?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Are there good examples on the effectiveness of these programmes in terms of skills transfer and capability through our local workforce?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Ministry projection for such programmes and how we can create interest and encourage more local workforce to seize such opportunities at the earliest possible time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, the PMET jobs which we used to do from the comfort of our offices and now in our homes, are at risk of being outsourced.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even before this, companies around the world are delegating small-scale projects to cheaper labour in developing countries, such as design, coding and customer services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Amidst the pandemic, technology has made it more easy to do remote work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, Singaporean talents would also have more opportunities to work remotely for foreign markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Certain essential services usually carried out by foreign workers had to be suspended or reduced in frequency during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is therefore prudent to push for skills development amongst the blue-collar sectors in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some of these jobs in construction, landscaping and cleaning are considered skilled labour in other developed economies like Japan and Norway.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening to observe that some young Singaporeans are embracing opportunities in the cleaning and waste management sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But such industries are still plagued with stigma and looked upon unfavourably.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we transform these sectors, along with mindsets, to ensure we always have a reliable pool of local talents to count on for these essential services?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A feature of the COVID-19 economic health shock is that it is uneven across sectors.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The issue to be raised here concerns the nature of help that might be offered to facilitate reallocation of workers out of the contact-intensive sector such as aviation/aerospace and tourism related activity into other sectors should restrictions on international travel make it unlikely for normal business to resume soon.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: More broadly, how do we prepare workers to minimise the scarring effects of a prolonged slump?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is useful to think about three groups of workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Those currently employed in the contact-intensive sector, those employed in the rest of the economy and new graduates who are entering the workforce.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, workers who are currently employed in the contact-intensive sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The JSS keeps these workers on the firms' payroll because the ultimate recovery of the affected sector avoids the need to incur investment costs to retrain a new group of workers with the necessary industry specific skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Workers in the aviation/aerospace industry will no doubt use the lull period to undergo training to deepen their skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps new developments in artificial intelligence and the technology embodied in Industry 4.0 can be mastered to position the industry to ride the wave of opportunities when more normal international travel resumes.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Firms employing workers in the tourism related industry working in tandem with their trade association and chambers can potentially take advantage of a home market effect to cater to demand from residents who are unable to travel overseas for their family holidays due to the pandemic.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: They can also encourage their workers to build upon common digital platforms to reach overseas customers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, workers were employed in the rest of the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), it has been observed that even though the measured rate of unemployment in the advanced economies decline, the employment to working-age population ratio had actually fallen below pre-GFC levels.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So the unemployment rate was low, but the employment to working age population was actually low as well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That is because even after several years subsequent to the Global Financial Crisis, there was an inadequate supply of good jobs offering good pay so that discouraged workers withdrew from the labour force.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, new graduates entering the workforce during COVID-19.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Holding a job confers benefits that go beyond the pay.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It provides also non-monetary rewards, non-pecuniary benefits of a job.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, being unemployed produces not only personal costs, but also has important social costs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Family members are also badly affected when a breadwinner loses a job.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The SGUnited Traineeship programme is also valuable in helping to link graduates from the Institutes of Higher Learning to potential employers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: During a buoyant market, a graduate holding an undergraduate degree might defer post graduate training.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the current labour market conditions, the opportunity cost of doing a full-time postgraduate degree is lower, lower than during the pre-pandemic era.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The Government might consider sharing in the cost of postgraduate education with firms in the potential growth sectors who might be willing to make contractual arrangements to partially fund the workers to acquire advanced skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: After obtaining the postgraduate degree, the worker is then employed by the sponsoring firm.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To sum up, the COVID-19 shock might turn out to be prolonged in this climate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is vital to minimise the scarring effect on a resident Workforce.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Deputy leader, would you like to move a Motion for exempted business for the Committee of Supply?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We aspire to be a greener nation and successful transformation necessitates getting everyone on this journey.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is inevitable that certain industries face decline while other industries such as those supporting the Green Plan will see an increase in demand.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What about the impact of disruptive technologies like driverless vehicles and drone deliveries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Bridging between the contracting and emerging industries will be challenging and it would be erroneous to assume that everyone can make the transition smoothly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our ITM and green plan should purposely feature this group of workers so that the industries can proactively redesign jobs to ensure inclusive growth in the post-pandemic economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, our 270,000 SMEs in Singapore represent 99% of all companies in Singapore and are arguably the heart of our Singapore economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In turn, our hardworking and loyal SME workers are the beating hearts of our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the world adjusts to the new landscape that COVID-19 has brought about, SMEs and our SME workers, more than ever, need to pivot, upgrade and keep relevant with the changes to keep afloat and to come out of COVID-19 stronger and better.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the heart of the pivot, the unions believe that two things must happen: (a) the uplifting and upgrading of our workers to be a dynamic and adaptive workforce to drive the much needed pivot that many SMEs need now; and (b) the building of an even stronger Singapore Core that will allow our SMEs to weather this and other future economic storms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Corlison, or better known by their Pearly White line, is a progressive SME in the Labour Movement family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As part of preparing for the new economy, Corlison's staff attend courses in Google AdWords and analytics training to enable them to receive competitive wages and grow to be even more future proof.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Corlison has weathered the COVID-19 well and continues to grow market share both here in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have built a strong Singapore Core through redesigning jobs, upgrading work processes and upskilling their workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SMEs like Corlison must not be an exception.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What will the Minister for Manpower do to assist SMEs in job redesigning and to uplift our workers so that they remain relevant and an important pillar for SMEs to be able to pivot?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Picking a leaf from our recent experience with the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme (SIRS) and the growth trajectory of freelance workers or what many call the "gig economy" workers, the Labour Movement hopes more can become union members and enjoy the plethora of offerings NTUC and our unions offer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At present, the Trade Unions Act requires a person to be in a "contract of service" to join a trade union.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Freelancers who are in a "contract for service" may not be full-fledged union members per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: While some own-account workers are truly independent, such as working proprietors, there are many who offer services as part of a wider organisation, such as taxi drivers, private hire car drivers and food delivery riders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has arguably pushed more workers into the so-called gig economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Moreover, the own-account worker's income is subject to incentive structures which companies can have the power to change at any point in time, without notice, and often do not require consent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Many of these workers end up stuck in the cycle of insecure work, reducing their opportunities for career advancement and, as access to credit is restricted, exposing them to greater risk of financial shocks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For many of these own-account workers, especially in the ride hailing and delivery industries, they exhibit many employee-like characteristics such as working exclusively for one company and/or having fixed working arrangements and key performance indicators (KPIs) which are tied to that of the company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Singapore's economy is built around a strong Singaporean Core and supplemented with migrant workers in specific industries and jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a business owner, I support the PWM.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In contract, PWM factually is a progressive and sustainable model where wages are paid in tandem with the necessary skills and productivity required for a specific sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers are showing that they do care about our lower wage workers and their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to have advanced conversations with industry partners to prepare employers so being ahead of the curve is necessary.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, the PWM is implemented by sectors, which is a vertical approach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also need a horizontal approach to include smaller enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Smaller businesses do not have economies of scale and do need a longer runway to prepare and scale up to pay their workers and concurrently remain viable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we celebrate our successful inscription onto the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural of Humanity and appreciate our hawkerpreneurs, we must recognise that they cannot offer the same salaries and benefits as other food operators such as restaurants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I spoke to Mr Lennon Peh, a hawkerprenuer in Bukit Panjang who sells mee rebus and mee siam.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He shared that his largest operating cost today is manpower cost, ahead of ingredients and rent.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He is also facing higher cost of cleaning and dishwashing and finds it difficult to make up cost by selling his mee rebus and mee siam at a higher price.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In his own words, "a hawker centre is meant to provide affordable food to Singaporeans and I will cause disappointment to customers if I increase prices." There are clear challenges in passing on costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, we need to consider that any cost increase to adjacent verticals will affect another sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we progress economically, I urge the Government to work together with the industry players to go into more details, to carefully and sensibly curate and develop bespoke PWM strategies to support all Singaporean business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Now, allow me to focus on our foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MOM has two main levers for managing our jobs and employment and they are the foreign worker levy and Dependency Ratio Ceiling (DRC).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our foreign manpower policy has worked well for Singapore to strike a balance in providing jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans and concurrently supporting the economy with adequate manpower to continue businesses, thereby, economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, we must continue to finetune our foreign manpower policy to ensure relevance and calibrate it to meet changing socio-economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And as they grow, more good jobs will be provided for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a business owner myself and through conversations with other business owners, the severe challenge of our current policy is the inability to first find the necessary local manpower to grow the business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my maiden speech, I suggested that we need a different approach for firms re-starting and pivoting after the challenges of 2020.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Manpower resources are necessary for these businesses to pivot, and the adjustment of levy is a temporary measure to assist them to have interim stability of their manpower base to transit.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perhaps, adopting a pilot approach with a few identified companies could yield greater insights and allow us to test such options first.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, I would like to propose applying and calibrating DRC in accordance with sub-sector nuances and differentiations, in particular, the services sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The services sector forms a large part of our economy and a differentiated quota would be more targeted and beneficial.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Each sub-sector has different job demand among Singaporeans, and businesses in each sector have various abilities to adopt automation to reduce manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that our relentless focus to accelerate the PWM adoption plus this fine-tuning of our foreign worker policies will be important levers to prepare us for a better future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, in October 2020, I called for a mix of fixed-term and non-fixed term work passes for foreigners, to attract investments in next-generation industries and stave off job displacements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a mix could be offered to investors for specific projects, especially in highly desirable future-ready industries where Singapore has competitive advantages.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The mix could be tweaked, depending on the degree of international competition for that investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For fixed-term foreign work passes, the foreign worker would be hired for a fixed term of, say, five years, for example, and this time would be used to train up Singaporeans with equivalent skills.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After the fixed term, hopefully, there will be enough Singaporeans with the relevant skills to replace that foreign worker.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This shares similarities with the Temporary Skills Shortage Visa in Australia where, if appropriately skilled Australian workers cannot be found, employers can bring in skilled workers for a fixed period.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, the Employment Pass scheme aims to train Singaporean citizens and upgrade their skills, fixed-term work passes meet precisely the same.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that the current work pass scheme such as the employment pass and newly-launched Tech.Pass aimed to attract skilled workers redressing skill shortages.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, more can be done to train up a Singaporean Core in next-generation industries and incentivises employers to hire Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, while the Tech.Pass is targeted at the movers and shakers of the tech world, fixed-term work passes target or broader spectrum of skilled workers across disruptive industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For fixed-term work passes, firms should have action plans for capability transfers to equivalent locals as well as mentorship schemes if feasible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Training can be tied to existing schemes in workplaces or academic institutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Extensions to fixed-term work passes can be considered in the case of very extreme extenuating circumstances.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, there are some jobs that Singaporeans are just not interested in.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my engagements with residents, I know that some would shun jobs in the marine, off-shore, maritime and manufacturing sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some parents would even hope that their children working as safety supervisors, engineers and technicians could change to safer occupations or office jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Within the sector, electronics, precision engineering and food manufacturing had the greatest number of available openings.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We can do all what we can to persuade, to promote these jobs but Singaporeans are just not interested in taking up jobs in these sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If these sectors are not able to attract sufficient Singaporean workers despite job redesign, improved wages, then their business operations would hit a standstill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Where there is justification given by these employers, can the MOM consider giving more latitude for the issuance of S Pass and Employment Pass so that the business can keep on going?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, while the Workers' Party welcomes the recent tightening of work pass requirements, there remains a need to review other aspects of these requirements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One aspect is the issue of unaccredited certifications, which has been in the news again of late.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Holders of certificates from degree mills and unaccredited schools have perplexed Singaporeans in previous incidents and may uncertain the belief that all our work pass holders can do the job they claim to be able to do on paper.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To be clear, such academic qualifications may not be forged and we have a system in place to deter forged qualifications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, these unaccredited qualifications are viewed with scepticism by our citizens and the various degree mills that offer academic degrees and diplomas for a fee with little to no real coursework, give little confidence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While MOM has indicated its risk-based approach in dealing with such matters and employers do have a primary responsibility to ensure the authenticity and quality of the academic qualifications submitted, this approach should improve so that the trust necessary for Singaporeans to accept truly talented foreign PMETs in Singapore can be improved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Therefore, I urge MOM to consider mandatory Educational Credential Assessments, or ECAs, for all Employment Pass and S Pass job applicants that need University degrees and diplomas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The cost to be borne by the applicant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such ECAs would only be accepted from a panel or Government appointed established independent consultants.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The ECA report will be sent to the relevant agencies, the prospective employer and the applicant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is not a novel idea since our medical and legal professionals have a list of recognised institutions that have only recently become narrower to uphold the standards of professions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Minister to look into this.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, COVID-19 has had a major impact on the way of life for many of us including that of our foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: During the pandemic, NTUC's Migrant Worker' Centre worked hand-in-hand with our stakeholders on the ground to contain the outbreak in the migrant worker dormitories.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This experience had brought to light the problems faced by our migrant workers in their dormitories, and underscored the immediate need for us to improve their living conditions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes the need to review how foreign worker dormitories are regulated, and if these regulations should be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In view of the challenges faced during the COVID-19 pandemic, I would like to ask MOM if there are any plans to further regulate the living conditions of foreign workers in dormitories that house lesser than 1,000 workers, such as increasing the scope of FEDA to smaller dormitories.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Chairman, SMEs in Singapore are among one of the worst hit by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially those whose workers are housed in dormitories.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I am fully supportive of giving our foreign workers better living conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: We value them and we must treat them humanely and give them proper housing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: JTC used to run these dormitories before they were privatised and taken over by commercial operators.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In the 1970s, to attract labour for the industrial estate, flats were constructed by JTC, which was responsible for developing and managing Singapore's industrial estates and their related facilities, was providing low-cost accommodation for workers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Will JTC help SMEs by coming back into this role of managing some dormitories?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: This can offer some competition with the privately-run dorm so that there could be healthy competition helpful for SMEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, it was disappointing to note that despite the pandemic exposing our vulnerabilities arising from our over-reliance on foreign labour, the Budget did not present new measures to fundamentally move our economy away from that over-reliance, apart from a tightening of the S Pass quota for the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would have been a golden opportunity to commence the needed restructuring, at a time when the size of our foreign workforce is down significantly, due to the pandemic, when businesses are looking for new ways to rebuild economic activities, a time for a "Reset", as Institute of Policy Studies, or IPS, calls it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With only minor tweaks to our work pass and work permit requirements, it is to be expected that the presence of foreign workforce in our economy will remain as large as ever.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite our objection to the continued over-reliance on foreign workforce, that is a matter of disagreement over what is the best policy for Singapore, and does not translate into disrespect for the foreign nationals working in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The contribution of foreign workforce to Singapore's development has been significant and they deserve to be protected as well, just like our local workforce.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our laws, such as the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF), the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, and the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act, are meant to prevent discriminatory practices and protect both local and foreign employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The severity of the COVID-19 pandemic's spread in dormitories has also exposed the harsh conditions many foreign workers live in, and exposed many inadequacies in the way we manage their welfare.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, instances of discriminatory hiring practices and violations of the FCF have been highlighted by the public.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given our large and growing foreign workforce, does the MOM have sufficient manpower and resources dedicated towards enforcing the relevant laws and regulations?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it able to assure Singaporeans that its resources have been put to good use, and that its enforcement has been effective?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moving forward, how will MOM manage the balance between local and foreign workforce to ensure they complement one another, not replace?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With reference to the recent discovery of work pass holders declaring qualifications from an Indian University selling fake degrees in their applications, how will MOM ensure the integrity of its list of accepted Universities and qualifications for work pass applicants?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the plan to prevent a recurrence of severe outbreak of contagious diseases in foreign workers' dormitories?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister update us on the improved standards for new dormitories and is the Ministry working on this in conjunction with NGOs?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much has been spent on rehousing foreign workers during this pandemic?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To protect our foreign domestic workers from abuse, will the Minister consider adding an item in the six-monthly medical examination report asking doctors to indicate if they noticed any signs of abuse?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Rachel Ong, if you would like to take your two cuts together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I wish to encourage our team with a story.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the peak of the pandemic, this volunteer asked a migrant worker who had been quarantined, if he had updated his family about his situation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He said no, he did not want his family to worry about him and added "because I'm in Singapore, I know I would definitely come out of this alive." To our MOM and MOH teams, thank you.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, the pandemic has revealed gaps in the living conditions of many of our migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There is more we must do for our migrant workers, not just in the interest of public health, but because it is the right thing to do for our fellow men.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My first cut relates to the regulation of living conditions in the Factory Converted Dormitories known as FCDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A visit to some kitchens in FCDs will reveal the presence of stray animals that roam freely as well as unclean food preparation and disposal areas.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A visit to some kitchens in FCDs will reveal the presence of stray animals that roam freely as well as unclean food preparation and disposal areas.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These kitchen spaces must be regulated to meet basic hygiene standards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second area for consideration is the persons-to-stove ratio.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Each day, migrant workers return from work in large numbers because of the long wait to cook.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some go to bed hungry as they would rather rest.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A sensible ratio of pax-to-stove will allow for better access for food preparation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For many, being able to prepare their own food is not just a matter of saving money but a small piece of comfort from home they taste at the end of a long day.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My second cut is on ensuring safe food access for our migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These meal packages include breakfast, lunch and dinner.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Caterers deliver their lunch together with breakfast in the morning, some as early as 5 am, which means that lunch is prepared way in advance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the worksite, lunch packages are often left in open spaces or under the hot sun because of the lack of food storage areas.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: When it rains or when stray animals get to them, the food is inedible and they go hungry.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Other times, they have hard, cold rice and sour vegetables to eat.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Such treatment of our migrant workers cannot and must not be tolerated in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For one, could we have employers provide lunch at the worksite?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is important that any increase in costs is not passed on to the already low-wage migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Access to safe food is a human right, not a privilege.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, the underpayment of foreign workers and Pass holders is not just a travesty against foreign workers; it sabotages Singaporean workers by undercutting their wage competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unscrupulous employers take advantage of the significantly imbalanced negotiating position of foreign workers and coerce them to return a portion of their salaries in cash.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Foreign workers are usually in debt by way of agency fees owed back home or to middleman employment agents, many of whom are outside Singapore's jurisdictional reach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The foreign workers in question would unsurprisingly be more concerned about their prospects for continued employment or employability in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such a scenario, the disadvantages of reporting an errant employer to MOM can far outweigh the advantages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The total number of foreign workers who were underpaid was not disclosed, nor were any details of restitution made to these workers disclosed as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister also shared that the number of errant employers caught was the result of improved detection capabilities and education efforts to encourage foreign employees to report salary irregularities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Minister committed that the Ministry would continue to take strong surveillance and enforcement action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, it is an offence if employers do not pay their foreign employees their contractually stipulated salaries or inflate their foreign employees' salaries with no intention of paying them the amount declared to MOM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second approach could be to tweak the law to require an errant employer, in addition to criminal penalties, to pay the foreign worker a penalty amounting to six months of the foreign workers' wage for each instance of intentional underpayment to circumvent MOM regulations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This amount would represent a punitive element that seeks to activate a behavioural effect to nudge foreign workers to proactively report employers who do not pay their declared wages, as required by MOM.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, if you would like to take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of them invest a significant amount of money to come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have to pay agent fees to even secure a job here.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means when they first step foot on Singapore soil, they are already thousands of dollars in debt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not enough to say that these fees were not paid in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These agent fees affect how effective our labour laws are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When migrant workers are saddled with huge debts, they are less likely to speak up against errant employers who flout Singapore’s labour laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Agent fees paid overseas undermine our labour laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOM also increase penalties for companies who are found to collect such kickbacks?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, this COVID-19 pandemic has shown that we need to do more for our migrant workers and I am glad we are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, the Foreign Employees Dormitories Act (FEDA) covers only licensed dormitories housing more than a thousand workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2017, I spoke up about the need to ensure that accommodation for migrant workers that fall outside FEDA are of equivalent standards to the larger dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, a dormitory housing 999 workers is no different from a dormitory housing more than a thousand workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM responded that FEDA imposes additional conditions on larger dormitories because of higher concentration risks there.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM also said that smaller accommodation types are still required to comply with comprehensive guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 has shown that we need to relook how we regulate risks in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More importantly, this is not just the issue of managing risk but of ensuring that every migrant worker helping to build our homes also has a decent home to return to at the end of the work day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that MOM will increase the coverage of FEDA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, migrant workers currently pay hefty agency fees to secure a job in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When migrant workers lose their jobs, they fall into heavy debt because they are unable to pay off the loans that they have taken for the agency fees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is perplexing that migrant workers bear the brunt of agency fees when it is common in many industries in countries for the employers to bear such fees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: MOM could consider setting up a standardised Singapore licence in mandatory online job portal for both jobseekers who are already in Singapore as well as overseas jobseekers who want to work as migrant workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Employers with quota in Singapore licence employment, agents should be the only ones allowed to advertise vacancies on the portal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Under such a scheme, it would be mandatory for the company and worker to transact the job application and acceptance through the portal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Alex Au of TWC2 and others have called for such a reform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Singapore licensed and regulated employment agents could still engage in bulk recruitment for specific end employers in Singapore, provided all recruitment goes through the portal for the sake of transparency to the worker, MOM and all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Such a portal may also be useful to enable the authorities and the workers themselves to track compliance with insurance requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After getting MOM approval for the workers, there is now an additional requirement for employers to apply for slots for their entry into Singapore on specific dates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was explained that there is a need to stagger the entry of foreign workers to reduce the risk of imported COVID-19 cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe employers understand the rationale, especially since Singapore has had a major headache dealing with outbreaks of COVID-19 in foreign worker dormitories.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The issue with the implementation is the uncertainty it creates for employers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For employers working on construction projects, not knowing when approved workers can enter Singapore, renders them unable to plan when work can resume.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some are working on key infrastructural projects which promise enormous social benefits, such as new MRT lines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Other employers might be waiting for new domestic workers to assist in desperate family circumstances.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, the workers in both the pest management and strata management sectors perform integral and important services.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Our pest management workers safeguard public health by providing essential services, such as preventing the spread of dengue and rodent and pest infestations, while workers in the strata management sector perform the important and demanding task of managing estates and providing all with a conducive and safe environment for us to work and play.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Some work has been done to acknowledge the essential work done in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The pest management sector was subsumed under the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map in the hopes of transforming and uplifting the sector to provide good and sustainable jobs to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In addition, the Facilities Management Skills Framework was launched in September of last year to provide the industry with information on the occupations, skills and competencies, and the possible career pathways available.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The development of an FMC Accreditation is also underway which will encourage higher management competencies and skillsets for workers in this industry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Arising from this agreement to raise the wages of Singaporeans and PRs in the lift and escalator sector, a move that all Singaporeans should support, it is inevitable that some maintenance costs for lifts and escalators will rise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The lift and escalator industry is one with relatively high barriers to entry and it is dominated by a handful of major players.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Some years ago, arising from a number of high profile accidents in the Town Council setting, many Town Councils moved to, as far as possible, tag the maintenance of their lifts to their original equipment manufacturers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This was also done in anticipation of a smoother rollout of HDB Lift Enhancement Initiatives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Currently, Town Councils are in discussions with various lift companies that seek to increase the maintenance costs of lifts in HDB estates arising from the implementation of the Progressive Wage Model in the lift and escalator sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In tandem, lift companies are also increasing the fixed schedule of rates for their lift parts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The latter move should not have any direct connection with the rollout of the Progressive Wage Model in this sector as the costs of spare parts generally rise in tandem with inflation, accounting for a reasonable 3% to 4% increase in costs for Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In my discussion with lift companies as an elected Member of Parliament of Aljunied/Hougang Town Council, the starting position of some lift companies has been to throw in a steep increase in maintenance cost.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The argument from some, when a minimum wage like the Progressive Wage Model is applied, is that costs will rise and the burden will have to borne by consumers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it would appear that some vendors could take advantage of the Progressive Wage Model to profiteer under the pretext of increased costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In view of the design of the Progressive Wage Model, and the extended conversations that take place between union representatives, the Government and the companies, I would like to know how the tripartite partners ensure that the prospects of profiteering by unscrupulous vendors is kept in check under the guise of rising wages for workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is especially in sectors like the lift and escalator sector where a number of the major players dominate and have a large footprint in that sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To this end, what role do Government bodies like the BCA, for example, play to ensure that the interest of Singaporean HDB dwellers and other consumers are protected from unjustified hikes in the guise of adherence to the Progressive Wage Model, in this case, in the lift and escalator sector?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Progressive Wage Model currently covers three industry sectors – cleaning, security and landscaping.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will cover the lift and escalator maintenance sector by 2022, and there are now discussions to implement PWM in six more sectors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share whether MOM has plans to roll out PWM in these sectors and, if so, what are the broad timelines for doing?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTUC wants to look at a vocational PWM for lower wage occupations, like clerks, general machine operators and electricians.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How does MOM plan to implement PWM for these vocations, given they cut across multiple sectors?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What levers will MOM use to impose wage, training and career progression requirements in the absence of licencing conditions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, how will the Government roll out the PWM differently so that it can be implemented at a quicker pace and made universal?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, which processes and requirements will be streamlined or removed to ensure a faster rollout?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We must do more to help our lower wage workers and I am glad we are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Workers within these sectors will welcome this news.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can we roll out the implementation of PWMs within a shorter timeframe?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With the expansion to these sectors, can MOM share whether all the 32,000 workers currently taking home less than $1,300 will be covered?

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you would like to take both your cuts, please do.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While main contractors have the resources to put in place comprehensive safety measures, these sub-contractors often do not.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many sub-contractors face manpower shortage during this period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Burdened further by the necessary safe management measures, sub-contractors often engage their own sub-contractors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am told that there can be up to four layers of sub-contractors at one major worksite.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This can sometimes lead to a situation where the eventual worker performing a high-risk task may not be qualified or trained to do so.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But developers and main contractors cannot lose sight of the one eventually performing the work underneath these layers of sub-contracting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many main contractors have been prosecuted for WSH lapses by their sub-contractors?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We last reviewed the penalties under the WSH Act in 2017.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is it time for us to review the penalties again?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also mandate developers to include a safety component in their tender specifications, budget and evaluation so that good safety measures will be a key consideration when awarding projects.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Often, parts of a major project are sub-contracted to freelancers and self-employed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge MOM to extend WICA coverage to them, particularly for high-risk sectors, such as marine and construction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must, therefore, ensure that our workers are well-rested so that they can concentrate on performing their work safely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope MOM can set clear guidelines on rest time for workers, especially at high-risk work sites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Also, there are only so many worksite safety inspections that MOM can do.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For WSH, workplace safety, to truly be pervasive, we need a dedicated WSH representative in every company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have spoken numerous times on this and I urge MOM to implement it quickly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We can upskill the Safe Management Officers to perform this role once the pandemic is over.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us ensure every worker returns home safely every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since the issuance of the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces, many have written to me to say that this is a step in the right direction towards de-stigmatising mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, they also expressed hope that more could be done to encourage better adoption of the Tripartite Advisory.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: MOM conducts the Comprehensive Labour Force survey yearly to help shape national manpower polices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can we include workplace mental health, in particular, the adoption of the Advisory's recommendations in these surveys to help track our efforts in building mental resilience among our workers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To drive full adoption of the Tripartite Advisory, we need to start in a targeted manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I propose we focus on the adoption of Employee Assistance Programmes (EAPs).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Among the small minority that do, it is common to hear that utilisation rate is low, due possibly to poor awareness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: EAP is important as it provides an avenue for the employee to seek support for any matters that affect their mental health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Companies that offer EAP report happier employees and an increase in productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope MOM can incentivise companies to provide EAP to their staff, by creating an early-EAP adoption incentive scheme to partially offset the “start-up” costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, workplace mental health issues are real and ever-present.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement is committed to protect the mental well-being of all workers, because Every Worker Matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It serves as a critical bulwark to protect workers against accidents, providing them important financial relief and some degree of protection in times of uncertainty and distress.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Even so, the central role of platform workers or gig economy workers in the economy over the last few years has shown no signs of abating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In a time of heightened retrenchment and lower salary prospects, such work provides an important outlet for many Singaporeans workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
