text: In this light, concerns abound over the lack of important worker protections for this group of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Workers are no longer confined to office cubicles, and close physical proximity is no longer a prerequisite for collaborative work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Employers are now trying to implement HR policies that strike a fair balance between work from home and work from office.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: For some, work from home has improved their quality of life while, for others, work from home has been very difficult to juggle as the lines between work and home are getting increasingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What is the balance point that is fair to both employers and employees?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: For example, for office employees or non-workmen that are on work from home but have OT pay in their working contracts, how do we remunerate such workers that is fair for both employers and employees?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can the Ministry ensure the rights of both employers and employees are protected through encouraging fair work employment practices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can the Ministry ensure that high productivity is maintained while encouraging and improving good work-life balance for our workforce?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: We must capitalise on this opportunity and ensure Singapore remains one of the more attractive places to work and, more importantly, retain the talent within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Fair work practices and a good work life balance will go a long way into ensuring our comparative advantage as we shift towards new working norms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Work from home has also demonstrated clearly how jobs can be done anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While we have debated extensively on foreign workforce quotas, let it not distract us from the fundamental question: how do we keep our workforce competitive and relevant in the global market, especially when workforce quotas are losing relevance in protecting jobs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we prepare, upskill and provide opportunities for our workforce such that we remain relevant in the global economy and not only do jobs in Singapore, but also do jobs for other countries remotely?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Can the Ministry or trade associations provide a platform for our remote professional services to be procured globally?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Remote working also requires a different set of skills for both the employer and employee, and an equilibrium of trust must be struck for it to work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Remote working managers must be able to set targets to manage the output of the team and not just manage the team purely based on counting the number of hours clocked.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: At the same time, employees must also not take advantage of the flexibility afforded to them due to remote working and be more self-directed in managing themselves to ensure that productivity is never compromised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Moving forward, even as we focus on investing in upskilling our workforce in terms of hard digital skills, let us concurrently promote the adoption and refinement of the softer skills of remote working to establish a suitably efficient and productive remote work culture environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: We should also consider how MOE can better prepare our children for a future of remote working.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We had promulgated the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment some years ago as well as rolled out outreach efforts and materials when the Protection from Harassment Act was introduced.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Perhaps, it is time to review this advisory and strengthen its legal and regulatory weight.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This also comes at a time when we see more Singaporeans undergoing PCPs, work trials, SGUnited programmes and traineeships in companies and businesses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is over and above the usual student interns and contract staff.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can we further enhance the protection and safeguard of the current employees as well as these new categories of workers in the workplace who may be subjected to workplace bullying or harassment or, worse still, sexual harassment, and other physical and non-physical abuse, including being made to work overtime and excessive hours without rest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As a nation, we must stop thinking of workplaces as a one-size-fits-all for all workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: With the new norm of flexible work arrangements and working from home, the notion of what is a workplace has been given a new breath of life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: A workplace can be in the office from 9 am to 6 pm or at home from 3 pm to 12 midnight.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Indeed, a workplace can be anywhere and anytime so long as there is Wi-Fi and a virtual background.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As such, these are exciting times for our women workers who are planning to return to work after a long hiatus because the typical nine-to-six office setting arrangement has never and could never work for them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Areas that need to be looked into are work-life harmony arrangements, fair hiring practices and performance evaluation criteria.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Comparisons, fair or otherwise, could be made between workers who work from home and workers who choose to work in the office.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Could I have the Ministry update us on what their plans are for these three points?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: To call this a cruelty would have been an understatement, and not to address this cruelty would be an injustice.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Imagine sending your daughter, wife or sister away to a foreign land in hopes of a better life, only to find out that she was treated this way.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As a whole, it is important to be consistent as a society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We cannot afford, on one hand, to celebrate the pivotal role FDWs play in the support eco-system and, on the other hand, remain lax on protecting the dignity and even lives of our FDWs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My resident, a new mother, recently quit her job.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because when she asked if a room at her workplace could be converted into a nursing room, she was told, "Why can't you just use the toilet?" Another resident struggled to find a job after she was retrenched. "Once you are a woman over 40, your value plummets.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, if you would like to take both your cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Given that there is a rising trend of dual-income families, I would like to ask if childcare leave can be extended on a per-child basis and up to the age of 12, as our Primary school-going children would see only a degree of care if they fell ill or simply to allow families to spend more time together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: With an increasingly ageing society, there is also the duty to take care of our parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The workplace has become more pro-family over the years, with more establishments offering various work-life initiatives, such as flexible work arrangements and non-statutory family-friendly paid leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Flexible work arrangements are important, no doubt, but it is also equally important to give our workers the flexibility to take time off without taking no-pay leave if required to take care of their children or parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Mr Chairman, while it can be argued that increasing leave provisions could be difficult against the challenging economic climate today, the challenges of our low fertility rate and ageing population are no less critical.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If we wish to uphold the ideal of family support and enable children to play their role as care-givers to elderly parents and for working parents to look after their young children while balancing other demands on their time, then the baseline level of parental care leave probably ought to be legislated to send the right signal to society on this matter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, flexible work arrangements come in a spectrum and, clearly, the level of flexibility that was in place pre-COVID-19 is dramatically different from what you have seen in 2020 and today, with work from home being the default work arrangement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Is it now time for the Government to reflect the needs of today's employees and employers and legislate a baseline level of flexible work arrangement?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Annual leave, sick leave, maternity leave and childcare leave are but amongst the various leave provisions currently legislated for under the Employment Act, although the right number is a separate topic for debate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It is not lawful for employers to give a notice of dismissal to a mother during her absence and neither is it conscionable for employers to discriminate against hiring women and mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Now, legislation is no silver bullet, but it is an all-important first step.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In the same vein, I do hope that the Government, businesses and society do not view flexible work arrangements as one which has unintended consequences of reduced employability and it is imperative for all of us and the Government to demonstrate leadership on this matter.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, our social safety net approach continues to put family as the first line of support.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is, these two dovetail into an untenable care load on women when it comes to elderly care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Because when we say "family", most of the time, it is daughters who end up caring for ageing parents.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As much as filial piety is a valued and important virtue in our Asian society, it should not come at the expense of one's old-age financial adequacy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mothers and daughters who care for children and elderly parents are facing poverty in their old age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For women who are in low-wage work, livelihoods can be lost for years, alongside with opportunity cost in CPF savings.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, the profile of those impacted by familial care is not homogeneous and there are also men whose jobs and careers are impacted by care-giving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are also men who are single fathers sandwiched between eldercare and childcare as their parents age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, we need differentiated policies for low-wage care-givers and those from higher income groups.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The savings reaped from reducing the need for institutionalised care for seniors, if transferred into basic income for stay-home care-givers, could help to save on long-term ComCare spending.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Through a basic income for care-givers, the narrative for their old-age financial dependency is shifted from "I am old and useless and dependent on welfare to feed me" to a dignified self-perception of "I am valued for the care that I provide and provided".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This goes a long way to instill self-worth in those who provide care for better mental health, dignity and self-esteem as they age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Carefare is a way to ensure dignified ageing for low-wage care-givers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This family care leave will ensure that both married people and single people will have leave they can use for any family emergency.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such simplification will also enhance the momentum by corporates to offer more autonomy to employees in how they manage their time, improving workplace satisfaction and also morale.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My hon colleague, Member Ng Ling Ling, spoke about getting AIC involved in the alliance of workplace improvements.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To prevent abuse of family care leave, we can require employees to register themselves as primary care-givers to their family members with AIC and allow firms to log leave utilisation on the same platform to qualify, perhaps, for Government incentives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Incentivising firms through corporate tax reliefs for family care utilisation may be one way to encourage more progressive workplace policies, leading to higher job satisfaction for employees and better mental wellbeing, which are both helpful for increasing productivity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge MOM, MOF, MOH and NPTD to consider these solutions together so that there is concerted effort to achieve our shared goal of a society made for families.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, if you would like to take all your three cuts together, please do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should legislate the same leave for all other workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to remember that this is especially important for essential workers who are unable to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also need to remember we have an ageing population and more and more of us will need time to look after our parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 has shown that work from home is possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many employers I spoke to said that they are willing to allow employees to work from home if the Government legislates this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not asking for employees to be forced to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that it is not possible for some lines of work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, I am asking for employees who can work at home to be allowed to work from home if they wish to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should also allow employers to reject such requests for business related reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many employees feel they are paid lower than they deserve because their employer mandated them to disclose their salary history.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I shared in this House that a ban on salary history disclosures has helped close the gender wage gap in California.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Josephine said that MOM would look at this study.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Deputy Leader, would you like to report progress?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) and other Members who have spoken passionately.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the COVID-19 pandemic, two battlefronts opened up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In terms of pandemic control, MOM was involved in managing the inflows of work pass holders and the outbreak in the migrant worker dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the economic front, we faced the sharpest employment contraction in decades.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In March last year, I had said that MOM would review the housing arrangements for our migrant workers, raise standards, improve well-being and be better prepared for a next pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Later, Second Minister Dr Tan See Leng will detail the steps we intend to take to transform the landscape for migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the jobs front, we have started 2021 on a firmer footing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Were this not so, we will be having a very different debate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Resident employment has rebounded to slightly above pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Resident unemployment rate has fallen since October last year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Throughout the crisis, our workforce has shown remarkable resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers too heeded the call to retain their Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On its part, the Government provided strong support for local employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many more Singaporeans stayed employed because of the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS), plus the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we tightened controls on foreign manpower to account for the slack in the labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But there is more work to be done.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unemployment and long-term unemployment rates are still elevated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even for those employed, some are in short-term or transitional positions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With this as backdrop, MOM has three overarching priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the short term, we must secure the rebound by shoring up hiring of locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Desmond Choo reminds us, we should not, for a moment, assume this will be easy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond immediate concerns, we must not lose sight of the medium and longer term.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Digitalisation, remote work, widening income gaps and an ageing workforce will continue to challenge us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must aim to overcome the crisis and help every segment of the workforce emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To do this well, our employers are critical.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Their capacity to innovate and become more productive will determine how much we can improve job quality over time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In supporting business transformation, we will pay particular attention to SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given the uncertainties that still persist, the job market may take a while to recover.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As announced by Deputy Prime Minister, we will extend the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa has asked how these programmes will help.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These 110, 000 represent roughly 5% of the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In two short months, such a movement into growing companies is not insignificant, especially when we consider the hiring weakness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: About half of the new hires were aged 40 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Prof Hoon Hian Teck will be interested to know that one-third of the JGI-supported hires switched into new sectors, possibly a re-allocation towards jobs with better future prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: JGI may also be helping to address the issue of unemployment and under-employment which Mr Patrick Tay was concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Around three in 10 JGI hires were not previously in a job; majority had been out of work for more than six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, the JGI uplifted those who were long-term unemployed as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More than six in 10, got the same or higher pay than their last-drawn.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To reduce scarring, we must be ready to deal with further displacements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Without JGI lubricating the process, the movement of workers into growing firms and industries will likely be slower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It comes on top of long-standing schemes like WSG's career conversion programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 2016, we have facilitated over 34,000 placements or redeployments through WSG's Career Conversion Programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Before 2020, WSG placed on average of 5,000 annually.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, we placed over 13,000, including a spike in re-deployments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This year, despite more subdued employer interest, we have catered capacity for 10,000 places.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Contrary to Dr Jamus Lim's suggestion, the Professional Conversion Programmes have well-documented outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: About 90% of the participants remained employed after 18 months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: About seven in 10 earned more than their last drawn salary.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Dr Lim can be assured that such conversion programmes will remain a core feature of our system of employment support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As for the JGI, this remains an extraordinary measure.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers should not delay their local hiring, in the hope that the JGI will be available indefinitely.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I hope Dr Lim agrees that some urgency on the part of employers helps jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, I hope employers take note of the enhanced support when they hire mature workers, persons with disabilities and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even with the substantial support provided under the JGI, we are realistic that not all employers can expand hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why we extended the SGUnited Traineeships, SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways and Skills programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will say more about the enhancements for the SGUnited Traineeships Programme and on the SGUnited Skills Programme at MOE's COS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For all unemployed jobseekers, until a suitable job materialises, these traineeships and attachments are the best way to be supported.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Prof Hoon thoughtfully highlighted the irony of unemployment insurance in heightening or even prolonging unemployment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unemployment or redundancy insurance, which Dr Lim also calls for, can indeed provide useful income relief.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But they cannot replace efforts to help people get back to work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Insurance payouts also may not match the allowances we are providing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many unemployed persons will not qualify for any redundancy payout.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They include new graduates just entering the workforce, workers who were dismissed, whose contracts ended and were not renewed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, we agree with Mr Patrick Tay not to foreclose these options.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the meantime, two key enhancements will make the attachments under the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathway Programme more attractive for mature individuals and their company hosts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With this enhancement, it is even more affordable to host someone with years of work experience than a new job entrant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To ensure that jobseekers can access help, WSG expanded its outreach significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the first time, career matching services were brought to the heartlands at scale, with the SGUnited Jobs and Skills centres in all 24 HDB towns.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is 70% higher than what we achieved in 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: WSG is continuing to innovate to provide better support to our jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: WSG has been and will always be a pathfinder for you.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, many Members of Parliament have asked what we can do to fortify our workforce in the post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have always operated on the principle of fairness at work, for both individuals and employers, to maintain cohesiveness in an open economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Every worker segment must have a fair chance to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Apart from securing the rebound, we will have five key thrusts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For lower wage workers (LWWs), we will focus on equality, mobility and dignity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For mature workers, we will address concerns over employability and retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For self-employed persons, women, and persons with disabilities, our focus is on inclusion and progression.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For our PMETs workforce, we need fair opportunities, quality and diversity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For migrant workers and foreign domestic workers, we need a renewed focus on safety, health and wellness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the years, our income gap has narrowed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Incomes at the 20th percentile grew faster than the median.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This decade, our ambition is to build on these gains and significantly grow incomes at the lower end.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Workfare, which the Government introduced in 2007, will remain a permanent feature of our social safety net, boosting incomes at the lower end and moderating inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But wages must go up, while preserving options to work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We agree with Dr Koh Poh Koon, Mayor Fahmi and Mr Pritam Singh that it is only fair for essential services workers to be better recognised for their efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a society, we must be willing to accord dignity through paying better salaries to those at the lowest end.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must also create pathways for these workers to progress.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am very glad Mr Raj Joshua recognises this as the true value of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: No one should dismiss its meaningfulness to workers, whatever the age of these workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why in October last year, with the encouragement of Deputy Prime Minister Heng, I sought the support of Secretary-General NTUC and President SNEF to set up the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower Wage Workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has developed an ambitious plan and detailed roadmap for a major expansion of the PWM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will start by introducing PWM to the food service and retail sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In cleaning, security and landscaping, in-house workers will be covered.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also work out ways to introduce PWM to other occupational groups, what Dr Koh calls vocational PWM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy who chairs the Workgroup will provide more details in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has what it takes to uplift the lives of our lower wage workers and their families.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In doing so, we will become a better and more cohesive society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, let me turn now to mature workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have tended to put everyone 40 and above into the same category of "mature workers".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, one can almost see two distinct generations within this group, with vastly different educational and work experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The group now aged 55 to 69 were born in pre-Independence Singapore, from 1951 to 1965.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One-third of this group have below Secondary school qualifications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fewer than 30% have a diploma or degree.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, given the widespread expansion of opportunities, nearly 40% hold PMET jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The group now aged 40 to 54 were born in post-Independence Singapore, from 1966 to 1980.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result of these differences, a 2019 MOF study had some interesting findings when it compared Singaporeans born in the 1950s and 1970s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In terms of median real income, the younger group earned twice as much as the older group when both were in their 40s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In terms of median real Ordinary and Special Account CPF balances, the younger group had three times as much as the older group.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the older age group, it is fair that they have the opportunity to work longer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will help them build up more for retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this regard, I fully agree with NTUC Deputy Secretary-General brother Heng Chee How and Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As earlier committed, the Public Service will proceed with these changes a year ahead of legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will help to keep us on track to raise the Retirement Age to 65 and Re-employment Age to 70 by the end of this decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Companies that raise their retirement and re-employment ages before it becomes compulsory, can apply for the Senior Worker Early Adopter Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many senior workers will work longer if they can do so part-time, they tell us that.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers that provide such opportunities can apply for the Part-time Re-employment Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Together with the support for job-redesign, which I will say more about later, this helps to address Ms Ng Ling Ling’s concerns about broadening the range of jobs for senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Interest in these two grants has been high.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But the larger goal is to create the momentum and shape a new norm among employers, where many more companies raise Retirement and Re-employment Ages to 65 and 70, well before 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A senior who can leave the workforce at age 70 instead of 67 and defers the start of his CPF LIFE payouts accordingly, can get around 20% more per month for life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part of the answer lies in raising CPF contribution rates for those aged 55 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Two years ago, tripartite partners had agreed to set in motion a phased increase, starting from 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Due to COVID-19, this was deferred by a year to avoid worsening the employment prospects of older workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fortunately, despite the pandemic, senior employment has largely held up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Tripartite partners therefore agree to push ahead, barring unforeseen circumstances, to raise senior worker CPF contribution rates from 1 January 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The CPF Transition Offset scheme will absorb half of the increase for employers in the first year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The impact will be further cushioned by the Senior Employment Credit which provides up to 8% wage offset to employers of senior workers for the next two years until the end of 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will study the extension beyond 2022 and will update in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As to Mr Louis Chua’s question on whether CPF members can earn higher returns, there is no magic formula.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Prior to the pandemic, we had been studying if a Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) can be introduced to help members who have the risk appetite and investment horizon but not enough investment knowledge.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need to update our planning assumptions and strike the right balance between risk and return in our design of LRIS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I seek Members’ understanding that we will update when ready.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Everywhere in the world, automation and digital advances have shifted labour demand towards higher level skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At all levels including PMETs, perfectly competent people can be at risk of displacement, unless they upskill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even in China, McKinsey estimates that up to 220 million workers may need to reskill for new occupations from 2018 to 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is almost 30% of the Chinese workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must try and make the best of these trends.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We can help our people pick up new skills and move into new jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With our strong educational foundation and build-up of the continuing education and training eco-system, we can turn this challenge into an opportunity for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By doing it better than other countries, we can strengthen our competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This must be complemented by new job creation and upgrading of existing jobs, both of which comes from pervasive business transformation, including that by the SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will say more about its nexus with workforce transformation later.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A previous survey in Singapore observed that our older workers are more dependent than their younger peers on employers’ guidance to attend training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Yet a recent study by the World Economic Forum suggests that in addressing new business opportunities, employers in Singapore are less likely than countries like Japan and Australia to re-skill existing workers, choosing instead to hire new staff who they can plug-and-play.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It must become the norm for employers in Singapore to build on the transferable skills of mature workers to meet new business opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we also need mature workers to take greater ownership of their skills upgrading.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A new norm of continuous re-invention must take root, as Ms Janet Ang also envisioned.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This year, we will introduce new programmes for in-demand jobs in growing sectors such as Manufacturing, Information Communications and Technology to provide fair opportunities for our mature as well as all jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The training and salary support in these programmes come on top of the enhanced JGI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, employers can get up to 95% of the costs covered.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is very generous and the right way to recognise employers and workers for making the effort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The full support and cooperation of all employers is critical to ensure the new policies benefit senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, the Government introduced the $1.3 billion Senior Worker Support Package to help companies adjust their operations to continue employing senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we will help employers defray the business costs of the increased CPF contribution rates for senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The goal of allowing our elderly to realise their dreams to continue contributing at work during their golden years and enjoy old age after retirement is not out of reach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As long as the tripartite partners, companies and the elderly work together, we will be able to build a fulfilling and fruitful golden era for the elderly in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In English): Sir, let me now signpost the direction for self-employed persons (SEPs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For well over a decade, our SEPs have consistently made up 8% to 10% of the resident workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are not a homogenous group and can be found in over 200 occupations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recent years, we have seen the rise of SEPs who use online matching platforms to get their work, or gig workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: About 3% of our resident workforce could be considered "gig workers".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They mostly worked as private hire car and taxi drivers, or drivers for delivery services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of their diversity, we should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to supporting SEPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we will support SEPs who wish to switch to regular employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One such example is Mr Nazry Zakaria, who transitioned from being a freelance project manager and set designer, to a Creative Strategist at Unearthed Productions – this is the name of the company.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To pick up digital marketing skillsets for his job, Mr Nazry participated in WSG’s Professional Conversion Programme for Digital Advertising Professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: His income is now more stable and he has better opportunities for career development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we have started to help SEPs better meet healthcare and retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the introduction of MediShield Life and CareShield Life, SEPs are generally well-protected against major medical expenses even without employer-provided benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The gap lies in the risk of income loss should illness prevent them from working, as SEPs do not have paid medical leave.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why we worked with insurers to introduce prolonged medical leave (PML) insurance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They now cover almost 40,000 SEP drivers and riders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also introduced the Contribute-As-You-Earn (or CAYE) scheme for SEPs providing services to Government procurement entities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With CAYE, SEPs have a convenient way to build up their medical balances.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2020, the first year of implementation, about 95% of SEPs remained on CAYE, although they could have opted out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They received close to $1 million in matched MediSave contributions from the Government, as part of a one-off incentive to help SEPs transit to CAYE.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nevertheless, we are aware that many SEPs had to defer their income and MediSave contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hence, we will extend the qualifying period to receive matched MediSave contributions for another year, till 31 December 2021, to provide more time for SEPs to fully benefit from this transition package.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the encouraging take-up of CAYE in the public sector, we will study if the scheme should be extended to SEPs serving the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will consult the relevant industry stakeholders before doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third area of focus is to find a better balance in the arrangements between “gig workers” and their intermediaries that deploy their services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Louis Chua had suggested, one way is to provide basic employment rights for SEPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In Italy, for example, “gig workers” dependent on one buyer or intermediary for their work, are categorised as dependent contractors and entitled to partial employment rights.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This provided added protection to the dependent contractors but also incentivised employers to reclassify regular employees as dependent contractors instead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In California, the legislative moves have swung like a pendulum.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as several MPs have highlighted, the latest ruling by the UK Supreme Court may have turned the tide decisively towards recognising Uber drivers as “workers”.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this regard, we welcome the NTUC’s keen interest to strengthen representation of SEPs and freelancers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In general, such workers can already form associations and be affiliated to NTUC.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples include the National Taxi Association and the recently-announced National Delivery Champions Association.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Likewise, in terms of work injuries, SEPs do have some protection.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Key platform intermediaries like Grab, Gojek and Deliveroo, already extend free personal accident insurance coverage to the SEPs who they place in jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, we acknowledge Mr Pritam Singh’s point that coverage is not uniform and collective bargaining is still not available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the Addendum to the President’s Address last year, we said that we would review the responsibilities of service-buyers and intermediaries to bring about a fairer and more balanced relationship with their self-employed workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In doing so, we will take into account the need to be fair, yet practical, recognising the usefulness of work opportunities provided by the intermediaries and the need to secure better outcomes for workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The views raised by Members on our foreign workforce fall into two broad clusters.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the one hand, Mr Edward Chia and Ms Cheng Li Hui suggested greater access to foreign manpower for some sectors, to address persistent shortages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the other, Mr Patrick Tay and Brother Abdul Samad emphasised localisation and strengthening the Singaporean Core, which requires reducing reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our fundamental objective is always to serve the interests of Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Access to foreign workers is meant to help grow a larger economic pie than we otherwise can.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, the foreign workforce must act as a complement to our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Work Permit level, the Services sector is our baseline for foreign workforce policies, with a Dependency Ratio Ceiling, or DRC, of 35%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Services account for three quarters of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We already recognise that some sectors are less attractive to locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Manufacturing, for example, has a DRC of 60%, at the operators' level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Construction, Marine Shipyard and Process sectors get even more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is a limit to how much further we can differentiate within Services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The sub-sectors, which lobby the hardest, already hire the big majority of work permits in Services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If we relax quotas for each one of them, it amounts to raising the overall DRC for Services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, as Ms Foo Mee Har has called for, we will focus on helping companies become more manpower-lean and strengthen their Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many firms have already started on this journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the last few years, we have also updated the S Pass policy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have made cuts to the S Pass sub-DRC in Services, Construction, Marine Shipyard and Process sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, we raised the S Pass qualifying salary twice last year and extended the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) job advertising requirement to cover S Passes to ensure that locals are considered fairly for these jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Hazel Poa expressed disappointment there were no more cuts other than for S Passes in manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Poa may not have been in Parliament for the last few years to know of all the adjustments we have made.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, I urge her to consider the points made by Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I would not say foreign workforce policies alone made this happen, but they certainly played a part.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to review our S Pass levers, including the qualifying salary, quotas and levies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be done together with efforts to transform industries and upskill the local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over this decade, employers should expect further changes to S Pass rules to be phased in.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I encourage them to start making the efforts to strengthen their local talent pipeline at this level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Employment Pass (EP) level, our aim is two-fold.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we will continue to ensure that foreign professionals complement our local PME workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The salary threshold is by no means a perfect gatekeeper of quality, but it is easy to understand and administer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We raised the qualifying salary for EP holders twice last year and will explore possible refinements to how we do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Janet Ang and Mr Saktiandi Supaat who spoke about worldwide shortages in tech and digital skills will understand why we do not set a quota on EPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Doing so will limit our ability to compete for the most cutting-edge investments and sophisticated activities, and hurt Singaporeans’ prospects in the longer term.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In any case, as Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Sharael Taha pointed out, knowledge workers can increasingly work from anywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This must temper our expectations regarding the usefulness of further EP controls, like levies, which Mr Leong Mun Wai has advocated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, we will ensure employers practise fair hiring and improve the diversity of their foreign PMET workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is wrong for employers to disregard qualified local candidates because of discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOS Gan will say more in her speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To comments by Brother Abdul Samad, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Pritam Singh regarding the Capability Transfer Programme (CTP), Deputy Prime Minister Heng noted that it is one of many to facilitate capability development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In general, we do not depend on any single programme to achieve better employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other agencies, besides WSG, have introduced or enhanced complementary capability development schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, ESG has the Global Ready Talent Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It supports Singapore enterprises in building young talent pipeline through internships and overseas work opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All the programmes that have helped to recruit, reskill or redeploy local PMETs, reduced the need to rely on foreign professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The supported projects span over 20 sectors, and we welcome more businesses to use it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For consistency with recent work pass moves, we will also regularise the work arrangements of Dependant Pass (DP) holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The vast majority of DP holders do not work during their stay in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: DP holders who have sought employment in Singapore via a Letter of Consent (LOC) constitute only about 1% of all Work Pass holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will provide sufficient time for existing DP holders working on a Letter of Consent (LOC), as well as their employers, to transit to this new arrangement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of them meet prevailing work pass criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those that do not, will have to cease working in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Transformation should serve a purpose to create better jobs, better skills and, therefore, better pay and better prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All of these cannot be achieved without better businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is why workforce transformation and business transformation go hand in hand.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many studies have attempted to predict jobs of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are useful signposts and help us create the conditions to keep businesses thriving.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we invest heavily to build up digital access and capabilities – Minister Iswaran said quite a lot about it yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, the extent and manner in which the future jobs materialise will depend on the entrepreneurial zeal of our businesses to disrupt the status quo and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To sustain better pay over time, there is no short cut to raising productivity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is rarely achieved by just up-skilling or re-skilling the workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the firm level, work processes must change and jobs redesigned.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the industry level, business norms must evolve and innovations embraced.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Again, these decisions depend very much on the dynamism and foresight of our business leaders, as pointed out by Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It includes dealing with the threats and opportunities of remote working within and across national borders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Strengthening business capabilities and promoting innovation comes within the purview of our sectoral agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM too, has a keen interest because the future of our workforce depends very much on it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On our part, we will pay particular attention to SMEs, a point which Ms Yeo Wan Ling has raised.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our partners, SNEF and many trade associations and chambers (TACs) tell us that SMEs face bigger difficulties in their quest to transform.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is understandable and we will help in several ways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2019, an interagency team, including the Economic Development Board (EDB), Enterprise Singapore (ESG) and WSG studied the impact of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) on the logistics sector in the next three to five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The study systematically identified how 56 existing job roles will evolve and how 12 new job roles will emerge.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As it turns out, more than half of the existing logistics jobs will experience a medium to high degree of change.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Logistics companies are taking reference from the findings to invest in new systems and reskill their staff.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For a warehouse supervisor, the job role can evolve from manually recording inventory to operating automated storage and retrieval systems.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, we have the ITMs and we have the JTMS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will help the TACs and SMEs alike with their workforce planning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, we expanded the Productivity Solutions Grant to also support job re-design.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is a panel of pre-approved consultancy firms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I urge businesses to take advantage of the enhanced support before it expires in a year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ultimately, their ability to transform themselves will spur our workforce to be transformed too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I have outlined MOM's priorities this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the short term, we will need to secure the rebound by shoring up hiring of locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the medium and longer term, we must help every segment of the workforce emerge stronger, including our migrant and foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will support our businesses to transform, especially our SMEs, so that we succeed together.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will keep strengthening fairness and support for workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Few countries have the extraordinary advantage we do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Without the reservoir of trust between the tripartite partners, many issues would not have been resolved quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In France, unions called for a nationwide strike to denounce the French government's pandemic response, disrupting essential services for many citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In Singapore, both workers and employers accepted the many painful adjustments we made.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Employers too helped to preserve a strong Singaporean Core, even if they had to downsize.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Once again, I thank Members for your many suggestions and support to MOM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic did not just test the resilience of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Tripartism was also tested and we are emerging stronger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, it has been over a year since the pandemic started.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been fortunate, with a whole-of-Government effort and everyone's support, patience and cooperation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: After successfully bringing the COVID-19 outbreak in our migrant worker dormitories under control, we continue to maintain tight measures to minimise transmission.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These include safe management measures, rostered routine testing every 14 days as well as through distribution of contact tracing devices to our migrant workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The CMP workers are the main occupants of our dormitories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With fewer workers and with more safe management measures, there have been significant project delays which impact completion timelines for on-going construction projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are now able to progressively bring in new migrant workers to support our businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This, by no means, represents that we have won the battle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, as I have alluded to in my previous speech at the end of last year, we have just reached base camp.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This base camp is different in that unlike Mount Everest or any mountain peak where we know where the full height of that peak is, for this particular crisis, we really do not know where that peak is.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Early this year, as the global COVID-19 situation worsened, we tightened measures to contain the risk of spread from imported infections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This further mitigates and minimises any risks of an imported case from transmitting the virus into the dormitories or into the worksites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Continuous adaptation and improvement have helped us to bring the pandemic under the current state of control.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But even as we continue to battle the evolving global and local situation, we continue to take on board the valuable lessons that we have learnt from the past many months of managing this current pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To prepare for future pandemics, we will transform our migrant worker landscape in three key areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we will fortify the upstream entry controls and measures for migrant workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is done so that we can minimise the transmission risks of new workers arriving on our shores and to ensure that they are properly onboarded before they move into our community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will strengthen the resilience of our dormitories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes conducting a comprehensive review of the housing standards of our dormitories, strengthening regulatory controls, to enable us to continuously raise housing standards across various the dormitory types and sizes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, we will also ensure the sustainability of all of our efforts to assure, to care for and to engage with our migrant workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will do so through cost-effective healthcare, establishing a migrant worker volunteer network to deepen our engagement with them, as well as partnering with our non-governmental organisations (NGOs), employers and community organisations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the first initiative, that of fortifying migrant workers' entry and onboarding process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Renewed inflows of migrant workers will be needed to continue to meet the needs of our growing economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But at the same time, we need to ensure that good public health outcomes are achieved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a one-stop centre to pilot an end-to-end onboarding process for all CMP sector work permit and S Pass holders entering Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are three elements to this: first, the Stay-Home Notice (SHN) period; second, an enhanced medical examination; and thirdly, an orientation and Settling-In-Programme (SIP) for these migrant workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The journey for a migrant worker to safely enter Singapore can be segmented into three zones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This refers to the upstream precautionary efforts in the source countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, before migrant workers depart for Singapore, they are required to take a COVID-19 Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test in their country and produce a negative PCR result within 72 hours before their departure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Robust pre-departure tests (PDT) will minimise imported cases and allow more workers to come in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are some employers already taking extra precautions in verifying the health status of their workers by even employing the use of serology tests before departure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is over and above the PCR test.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows employers to identify workers who have recovered from COVID-19 so that the public health measures that we are going to adopt on arrival can be more targeted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This refers to what we do here in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When they arrive here, we have introduced a combination of on arrival PCR test as well as serology tests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows us to better differentiate recent infections from the recovered persons can still be intermittently shedding the virus but they are no longer contagious.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, for these workers who are found to be already recovered, we can exempt them from SHN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this is where our one-stop MWOC comes in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This enhanced medical examination programme will entail more comprehensive and rigorous screening to enable appropriate health support and interventions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This enables us to identity these risks and have more effective targeted downstream patient care.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It also reduces potential work disruptions and unexpected medical costs for employers from untreated health conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, workers will learn to adopt the safe management measures, learn how to use contact tracing devices and SafeEntry check-in as well as the Foreign Worker MOMCare (FWMOMCare) app to monitor their temperature, update daily health status and access telemedicine if symptoms are reported.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our guest migrant workers will learn when and how to seek help when they are unwell or when they need assistance with employment disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This refers to the time when the workers have cleared all these check-ups and when they can move into their respective residences and adopt safe living measures both at work as well as in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This MWOC brings together various entry processes as one efficient, seamless, integrated end-to-end process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Centralising and coordinating the operations and functions together also facilitates faster reaction times as well as allowing us to adapt and be able to pre-empt better preparation for future pandemics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It benefits employers, workers and the general community in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For employers, bringing the processes together helps to lower the risk of transmission from imported cases, enabling the entry of more migrant workers to support our businesses where they are needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers, especially the small and medium enterprises (SMEs), will have the benefit of the MWOC providing an end-to-end SHN and onboarding service, compared to now, where each employer would have to arrange for the medical screening and Settling-In-Programme (SIP) on their own after their workers have completed their SHN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For workers, the onboarding programme will help them start their employment in Singapore on the right footing, with them knowing their rights.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The MWOC will also provide the flexibility to adjust SHN as well as testing measures in the blue zone, depending on the volatility and the fluctuation of the situation in the source country where they come from in the green zone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is done in order to safeguard the safety and the health of the workers as well as our general community in the white zone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim highlighted her concerns of households and businesses of the uncertainty when bringing in migrant workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This MWOC is part of our efforts to minimise COVID-19 importation risk and we hope that this will also serve to minimise other types of future infectious disease importation risks, so that we can bring in sufficient numbers of workers to support the needs of our economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We adjust the entry numbers in a very dynamic fashion – depending on the infection transmission risk in each one of the home countries, depending on the risk levels and the regions that our workers come from.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We facilitate the entry of foreign workers as required for key infrastructural projects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also been responsive and we have provided a higher degree of certainty to employers as well as households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Entry approvals are allocated on a first-come-first-served basis by the chosen arrival date, and we facilitate, where it is needed, families to come and enter together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Entry applications will get an outcome by the next working day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers will also be advised on the next available arrival window should applications for their chosen arrival dates be unsuccessful.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Louis Ng asked how we can and we will improve the standards of dormitories, including smaller sites as well as factory-converted dormitories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we have a variety of migrant worker dormitories – the Purpose Built Dormitories (PBDs), the Factory Converted Dormitories (FCDs), the Construction Temporary Quarters (CTQs) and the Temporary Occupancy License Quarters (TOLQs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All dormitories, whether regulated under FEDA or not, are subjected to a set of regulatory requirements set by the various Government agencies, covering areas such as building and fire safety, minimum living and hygiene standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: FEDA imposes additional requirements in areas such as public health and safety, security and public order, and the provision of social and commercial facilities as well as services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will allow us to bring the regulation of all dormitories – that means it covers the FCDs, the CTQs and the TOLQs – under one single Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are going to introduce consistency in terms of housing standards and safe living requirements in all the dormitories through this FEDA expansion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will allow MOM to prevent and more quickly contain disease outbreaks in the dormitories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Requirements to create more isolation bed facilities, stringent infection control measures, and ensure dormitory residents' well-being, had to be implemented on non-FEDA dormitories through the COVID‑19 (Temporary Measures) (Control Order).

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When we expand the scope of FEDA, this would empower MOM to directly and quickly impose safe living and infection control requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This also enables MOM to implement a consistent framework of housing standards across dormitories of different sizes and types.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will have common requirements that apply across the board such as cleanliness, space and ventilation as well as additional requirements that depend on the dormitory's size such as recreational facilities in some of the larger dormitories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will engage stakeholders in the coming months to review and to get their input in terms of expanding the scope of FEDA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and Ms Hazel Poa asked whether dormitory standards will be adjusted and how the higher costs arising from future improved dormitory standards will be managed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As most migrant workers continue to live in communal settings, it is critical to improve, better prepare and future-proof our dormitories for future pandemics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To respond to the immediate COVID-19 challenges while strengthening the public health resilience of our dormitories against infectious disease outbreaks and enhancing living conditions for migrant workers, we have piloted a set of improved standards at these QBDs to test for their effectiveness, their feasibility and their economic viability and sustainability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is in order for us to reduce inter-mixing amongst residents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Each QBD room is also fitted with en-suite toilets to minimise transmission risks from shared facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Kitchens, dining rooms and laundry areas also cater to smaller groups of residents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
