text: Because these are the kinds of technologies that would transform this sector, and not quite RPA/AI and advanced analytics.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The value of these kinds of studies is to look very specifically within a foreseeable time frame, technologies that will make a key difference to help the companies transform the jobs and to re-skill their workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I also like to thank Minister for Manpower Mrs Josephine Teo for responding to my Budget debate speech on the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think she gives some information with regard to how much has been expended on it so far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just going back very quickly to when the programme was announced in 2017, the former Minister for Manpower Mr Lim Swee Say, stated, and I quote, this was in the Budget debate of 2018, he said, "The scope of capability transfer is tremendous – high tech to high-touch; MNCs to SMEs; domestic to export-oriented industries".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we were given some information about the funding cap per project.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in exceptional cases, even more could be given if the particular project was worthy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I would like to ask whether it would be correct to characterise the Capability Transfer Programme thus far as a scheme for which there is more to be desired, in view of the amount of money that the Government has spent on it so far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because I would agree actually that there is a lot of scope for it to support and improve the prospects of the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question that I have is, again, with regard to the Capability Transfer Programme, whether there are plans to improve its usage across industries tracked by the ITMs because I would agree that there is a lot of scope for it to be a gamechanger.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think we had an example of it in the MTI COS where the Minister for Trade and Industry spoke about moving into a high-value bracket in manufacturing, for example; not just doing what other people are doing but doing things which very few people can do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And here, I believe the Capability Transfer Programme has a lot of scope.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Pritam Singh for his interest in the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Former Minister Lim Swee Say, at the launch, also made clear that the CTP is one of many programmes that the Government has to support capability development.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Specifically, he also highlighted that it will complement the other programmes that sector agencies already have in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of course, as the situation evolves, the sector agencies may identify more specific programmes that help their sectors to achieve better transformation and they make a case to MOF.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If MOF considers that those needs are better met by such sector-specific programmes, then funding would be provided and the sector agencies will run it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The CTP itself is not tied to any particular sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, in that sense, it is focused in its mission.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it can apply across sectors that are not covered very specifically by our agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I think it is a useful complement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I should also caution that, from time to time, the Government re-examines all of its schemes of support to businesses and streamlining happens on a regular basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, this is part and parcel of Government administration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Ministry for the replies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How many of those on the SGUnited Traineeships were offered full-time employment in the industry that they were doing their traineeships in?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, on senior employment, a lot of effort for senior employment is at the job-matching level at the local level.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry share more plans on this effort?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The trainees, being fresh graduates, are at the start of their working lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think all of us have had that experience and benefit from being exposed to a variety of employment settings and different kinds of industries, different types of companies – big companies, SMEs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And this experience is really meant to try and help the trainees build up their resumes so that when they advance to the next stage of seeking a permanent job role, they are able to tell the prospective employer that, "Look, this is what I learnt".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It matters less whether they go back to the same industry or same company, than the fact that they will be able to advance to a new job role.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think what we will want to watch very carefully is whether they are able to move to a job thereafter and that is what we will focus on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second question with regard to senior employment is that seniors are just like all other jobseekers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have aspirations, specific job requirements, and a variety of ways exist in which to help them to get into a job.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can come to WSG, they can come to e2i, depending on what kinds of careers they have been active in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even employment agencies might be a suitable avenue of support for them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As to local types of jobs, to my knowledge, whether it is the CDCs or even some constituencies, there are attempts to try and make available such jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Again, I think they are complementary and certainly welcomed in terms of providing more openings that seniors can consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have a quick clarification question for Minister Teo when she said that the Ministry would not close the door to suggestions like redundancy insurance, among other things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does that mean that there are, in fact, impending plans to set up a sort of a tripartite workgroup on, say, end-to-end job safety net or to further study the kind of feasibility of unemployment insurance schemes as well as other end-to-end job safety net schemes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I mention this because when I stated that we have the functional equivalent of this end-to-end job safety net, it was including a number of elements, such as the COVID-19 Support Grant or the Recovery Grant or SIRS, which, at the moment, are actually temporary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, it would be nice to understand the extent to which some of these schemes may have a longer shelf life.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, when the Government says that it keeps an open mind on issues, that is exactly what it is – it keeps an open mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It continues to look at the experiences of other countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It considers studies that are done elsewhere and also assesses, on a continuous basis, the changing landscape in Singapore and whether further action needs to be taken.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If and when there is a need to set up another tripartite workgroup, the Member can be sure that it will not be done in secret; it will certainly be announced publicly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The mental wellness of our FDWs is something that needs to be considered with care.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that their workplace is also their home, many FDWs find it hard to disengage from their work, especially if they are care-givers to the elderly and young in the households.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And NTUC's FDW clinics for employers and employees that I helm for the labour movement, an often brought up point is the loneliness that our FDWs face, particularly if they are first-time FDWs and they come from different cultures and speak only their native languages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In such cases, would the Ministry share with the House if there are plans to assist our FDWs in work-life harmony and if there are comprehensive outreach programmes being done by the Ministry to ensure the wellness and settling-in of our new FDWs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, actually, MOM has a number of measures already to help our foreign domestic workers adjust in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: These include educating them via the settling-in programme on matters, such as Singapore's social norms, their employment rights and stress management.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In addition, MOM works with stakeholders, including NGOs, to provide recreational facilities and stress management courses.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: NGOs, like CDE under NTUC, and FAST, each maintains a 24-hour helpline for foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: CDE also partners mental health advocacy organisations, such as Silver Ribbon, to provide counselling services for foreign domestic workers who need someone to talk to.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We recognise the importance of foreign domestic workers having opportunities to establish friendships, pursue recreational activities and deepen ties with the community.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, we work closely with partners, such as CDE and FAST, which I mentioned earlier on, to provide training, recreational spaces, social activities.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The wide range of services and activities available include befriender programmes, affordable educational courses, counselling facilities, libraries and gyms.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And there are many opportunities for foreign domestic workers to enhance their work-related skills or pick up new skills for their personal development.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We encourage our foreign domestic workers to utilise public parks and spaces as well and adhere to the safe distancing measures imposed at these public places, instead of gathering on public walkways where there may be safety and accessibility concerns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I think the first is regarding the LRIS which Minister Teo shared.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that this is something that has been in place, but it has been about close to five years since August 2016 when the plans were first announced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I was just wondering if there is any specific timeline that the Ministry could share in terms of when we can expect some of these details to be announced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And in relation to the cut I have filed, has the Ministry considered or is it considering allowing CPF members to invest alongside the Government's investment vehicles since we do not really need to look very far in terms of the options for funds that Members can consider.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to parental care leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is this something that the Ministry is actively looking at considering to implement in the near term to send a signal that this is no less of a need, as compared to some other leave provisions, such as childcare leave or even annual leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Chua had, during his cut, talked about CPF members co-investing with, I think, our sovereign wealth funds.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am not really sure whether he has fully thought it through because, in all investments, there are risks involved.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And our sovereign wealth funds have to take a certain amount of risk in order to generate the returns and, on a year-to-year basis, sometimes even over longer periods of time, there is no sure win, no perfect guarantee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, when we think of their good record of performance, we must also not forget that there are occasions where these investments do not produce the same returns, as hoped.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is something we always have to keep in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I beg the Member's indulgence that it is more important that we do a proper job than to rush it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Chairman, I have two clarifications for Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that the Senior Minister of State agrees with my suggestion to upskill SMOs to become WSH representatives in their companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The NTUC will work closely with MOM to push and facilitate this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some safety officers have raised concerns that their hands are sometimes tied when it comes to improving internal workplace safety practices in their companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They constantly worry that doing so will cause them to be blackmarked by their employers as workplace safety is always seen as a cost centre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They worry that speaking up may put their employment contract renewal at risk sometimes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State to respond to my question on whether we can better track the effectiveness of our workplace mental health initiatives and the adoption of our tripartite advisory on mental well-being at workplaces through perhaps the annual surveys that MOM conducts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, I thank the Member for his questions and I will start with the mental health question first.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the adoption of recommendations from our tripartite advisory on mental well-being at workplaces, including Employment Assistance Programmes (EAPs), which I know the NTUC has worked really hard on.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Since its launch in November, our partners and our mental health providers have reported increasing interest from employers in offering mental well-being initiatives at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think this is a very positive sign, given the current COVID-19 arrangements that we have.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the economy recovers, we expect more companies to reprioritise their resources to more mental well-being initiatives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Moving on to Mr Yong's second question on the audit that the safety officers do, rest assured.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is same as financial auditing, too, where they have a safety responsibility, like the fiduciary responsibility that auditors have, to report any risk to the safety of our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are two things that workers can do.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One, they can use the SnapSAFE app which is available.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Two, they can call the MOM safety hotline which is at 6317-1111.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Do call if you have any information which we can look into.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I can assure Members that following many of the incidents, we are definitely concerned of late, especially with contractors rushing to catch up after work stoppages last year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think that is one risk that we saw.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The second one is certainly manpower disruptions, as I have mentioned earlier, due to border controls and pandemic measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we need companies to put in place adequate risk assessment measures to adhere to safe work processes and ensure that, when there are machines, they are only operated by staff that are trained.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On MOM's part, we are putting in place more technology for the industry to adopt, such as drones, to replace workers from difficult high-rise inspections so that it makes their work safer.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Two, fleet safety technology, for example, can improve situational awareness of drivers and wearables, too, that can monitor workers' health.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On our part, when it comes to enforcement, we have also been using behavioural insights to target riskier firms.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For construction, for example, MOM highlights to companies how their safety records faired relative to industry peers and calibrates our inspection frequency based on their standing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For manufacturing, transport and storage sectors, MOM uses big data to predict riskier companies and focuses inspections on them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Data models are refined continually to improve our enforcement.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have also started publishing WSH learning reports.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, addressing risks of slips and falls as well as in inhaling toxic fumes from detergents and working from heights.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, these are some of the measures that we are putting in place to make Singapore a safer place for all workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, I thank the Ministers and Ministers of State for all the work that MOM is doing for the workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this a conscious trade-off that we have to make?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question: given that the Ministry has already done a lot of work on the PWM – and I appreciate the work that the Government has put in and this House is also of a consensus that all of us should be helping the lower wage workers more – so, why is it so difficult to take that one small step because we have already put in a lot of subsidies for the low-wage workers, just take that one small step to make it a blanket living wage or minimum wage?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And then, we can concentrate our effort and resources on upgrading our workers through the vocational PWM that the Government has started.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think that is a very good step because we really have to upgrade the skills and the income of our higher wage workers actually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Leong for his acknowledgement of MOM's work and also for his support for extending the PWM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He has asked the question: why do you not just take that small step?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think, first of all, we have to recognise that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is the broadest-based support that we are providing to lower wage workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It comes every month; it supports the lower wage workers, not only cash payouts but also to build up their CPF so that, like all Singaporeans, they have the prospect of not just providing for their families but also providing for themselves in retirement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What happened to our resident workforce, local workforce?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It actually grew, very modestly, but it grew.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Which country can actually produce this report card?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, from that perspective, in what way has the local workforce been disadvantaged?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, let me declare that I am a council member of Singapore Business Federation (SBF).

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, Minister Josephine, if I can tell you, my niece took a traineeship and then she found a job.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am sure her cohort who did that would be very appreciative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the NTUC's call to do this in two to three years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, SBF fully supports all the efforts to uplift our lower wage workers, especially with Workfare and PWM.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I think I shared the national business survey by SBF.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The time horizon for global recovery, of course, we all know, is uncertain and, according to some global watchers, it could be as long as four to seven years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke to my Mckinsey friends and they have got a big scenario planning thing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, their worst scenario is four years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Since we are in pandemic mode, I guess we should take the worst – it will be about four years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, while I would like to see our low-wage workers earn more – and believe me, you, I really want to see that – but it may be early for our companies recovering from disruption to take on additional wage hikes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, in my view, keeping jobs ought to take priority over wage hikes at this time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the small businesses are still struggling and, with the DRC and if plus wage hikes, they are going to quit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our low-wage workers will only have wages if there are at least companies to work for.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For those who understand the lingo, I am having an Isaac moment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ang, can you come to the point?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, I appreciate that MOM has had the unenviable task of balancing multiple demands.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And SBF and the business community have pledged in the Sustainability Employment Report in 2019 to support opportunities and progression for our workforce, especially the vulnerable workers and the low-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: So, I advocate for continued dialogue amongst all members in the tripartite workgroup (TWG), on a timeline that can be a win for all.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, I note there is time constraint, so, I am just going to keep it short.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, I thank the Member and SBF for supporting the initiatives of our tripartite work group.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that is precisely why PWM takes a very sectoral approach in which, we have just announced that we are setting up the tripartite cluster to study this for the Food and Beverage as well as the Retail sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We fully understand the challenges of the sectors today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is why we have made a conscious effort to hold back by a year, before we set up the tripartite work group to understand this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And rest assured, as said in my speech, we will look at the differences in the two sectors and the different business models that may occur.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Even for the retail sector, we are mindful that there are also threats from e-commerce and therefore, we are also looking at the whole sector as a whole.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are adaptations that we have done in the past PWMs and we will continue to do so to study and adapt to every sector as required.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Desmond Choo, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Chairman, I would like to thank Minister Josephine Teo, the public office holders, Permanent Secretary Aubeck Kam and the team of MOM officers for their ceaseless work over the last 14 months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: They had been at the frontlines of COVID-19 and most of them still are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We know that many challenges and long hours await them as Singapore seeks to recover from the pandemic and tackle the structural forces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: For that, we want to place on record for appreciation for the MOM officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: On that note, Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
